title: Remote & Distributed Locks (Needed in Distributed Transactions)
summary: Distributed locks don't give you mutual exclusion — leases plus fencing do. When and how to use them without corrupting data.
topic: Fault and Failure Tolerance + Distributed Consensus

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: A distributed lock is **not a lock. It is a lease with an expiration**, granted by a third party that can be wrong. If your correctness depends on exclusion holding *after* the lease expires, you have already lost. The only safe design is **lease + fencing token checked by the resource itself** — everything else is optimisation, not safety.
What it is, precisely

A distributed lock gives you **best-effort single ownership of a named resource across processes that share nothing** except a coordination service. One holder at a time may act on `order:8421`, `job: nightly-rollup`, or `account:87` while others wait, back off, or fail fast. The lock server — Redis, ZooKeeper, etcd, a database row — records `resource -> owner-token + expiry`. It does not block threads. It does not stop a paused process from waking up and writing. It just answers the question *who holds this name right now, as far as I know*. That gap between *as far as I know* and *what is actually true* is where every outage lives. Choose the implementation based on what happens when that gap opens: nothing much, or corrupted state.

Split every use into two buckets, because they demand opposite designs. **Efficiency locks** exist to avoid duplicate work: run the cron on one node, suppress the second email, coalesce cache refreshes. If exclusion breaks and two nodes do the work, you waste money or annoy a user — nothing corrupts. A single Redis `SET NX PX` or a database row is plenty here, and quorum buys you nothing. **Correctness locks** exist to prevent two writers from interleaving updates to shared state: deduct inventory, mutate a file, drive an external actuator. If exclusion breaks, you get lost updates, split brain, or irreversible side effects. For this bucket a bare lock is **never sufficient**, no matter how many nodes run it. You need a lock service with strong consistency *plus* a fencing mechanism at the storage layer. Interviewers dock you for confusing the two — proposing ZooKeeper for duplicate emails is over-engineering, proposing single Redis for ledger writes is a correctness bug.
The mechanism: lease, heartbeat, release

Nobody implements a blocking distributed mutex. What gets built is a **timed lease**: acquire if absent, renew by heartbeat, expire automatically so a dead holder cannot block the system forever. The `TTL` is the core trade-off. Short TTL means fast recovery when a holder crashes — but forces frequent renewals and raises the chance a slow or paused holder loses the lease mid-work. Long TTL means stable ownership during GC pauses and network blips — but turns every crash into minutes of unavailability. That is why every serious library couples a short TTL (5–30s) with a background renewal thread that extends only while the holder is alive and healthy, and stops on shutdown or pause. Release must be **owner-checked**: delete only if the stored token still equals yours. Release without a token check lets a stale holder delete its successor's lock, collapsing exclusion exactly when you needed it.

blocks.title: Lease lifecycle
blocks.caption: Acquire with token, extend by heartbeat, release by compare-and-delete.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A["Client generates random token"] --> B["SET lock-key token NX PX=TTL"]
  B -->|"key absent: acquired"| C["Do work, renew TTL in loop"]
  B -->|"key present: denied"| D["Backoff, retry or fail fast"]
  C --> E["Release with Lua: delete only if token matches"]
  C -->|"crash or stop renew"| F["TTL expires, next waiter can acquire"]

import uuid, time, redis
r = redis.Redis()
ACQUIRE = "return redis.call('set', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'NX', 'PX', ARGV[2])"
RELEASE = "if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end"

def acquire(key: str, ttl_ms: int, wait_ms: int) -> str | None:
    token = uuid.uuid4().hex  # owner identity, never reuse
    deadline = time.monotonic() * 1000 + wait_ms
    while time.monotonic() * 1000 < deadline:
        if r.eval(ACQUIRE, 1, key, token, ttl_ms):
            return token
        time.sleep(0.05)
    return None

def release(key: str, token: str):
    # WHY Lua: GET + DEL must be atomic, else you delete your successor.
    r.eval(RELEASE, 1, key, token)

blocks.title: Never DEL a lock you did not verify
blocks.text: `GET` then `DEL` in two round trips is broken. Between your `GET` and your `DEL` the lease can expire, a second client acquires it, and your stale `DEL` removes *their* lock. Both clients then believe they hold it. The fix is mechanical: **store a random token on acquire, compare-and-delete with a script on release**. If your client library does not do this, replace the library.
Why TTL alone can never be safe: fencing

Leases expire while work is still in flight. A process suffers a 15-second garbage-collection pause, its TTL lapses, a second process acquires the same lease and starts writing, then the first process wakes up *still believing it holds the lock* and writes anyway. No lock service can prevent this — from its viewpoint both acquisitions were sequential and valid. Clocks make it worse: if the holder's clock jumps or Redis's `EXPIRE` fires early relative to the holder, the window of dual ownership widens silently. The trade-off is brutal and unavoidable: you need expiry for liveness (crashed holders must not wedge you), but expiry destroys safety (live-but-slow holders become impostors). The way out is to stop asking the lock service to guarantee safety. Let it provide **liveness and ordering**, and push **safety down to the resource** with a monotonically increasing fencing token. The lock service hands out `1, 2, 3...` on every grant. The storage layer persists the highest token it has honoured and rejects any write with a smaller one. A stale holder's writes then fail closed even though it still thinks it is the owner.

blocks.title: Fencing blocks the stale writer
blocks.caption: Lock service orders holders; storage rejects old tokens.
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  L["Lock service: counter 1, 2, 3"] --> A["Client A gets token 1"]
  L --> B["Client B gets token 2 after A stalls"]
  A -->|"write x with token 1"| S["Storage: max seen = 2"]
  B -->|"write x with token 2"| S
  S -->|"reject 1, accept 2"| R["One winner, no corruption"]

# WHY fencing: the resource, not the lock server, enforces exclusion.
# Lock service must return a strictly increasing fence token per grant.
# e.g. ZooKeeper sequential node, etcd revision, Redis INCR, DB sequence.

def guarded_write(db, key: str, value: str, fence: int):
    # Atomically: reject if fence <= stored_fence
    updated = db.execute("""
        UPDATE records SET data = %s, fence = %s
        WHERE id = %s AND fence < %s
    """, (value, fence, key, fence))
    if updated == 0:
        raise StaleOwner("token expired: another holder superseded you")
    return True

blocks.text: Implementations, honestly compared

blocks.caption: Pick by consistency need and failure budget, not by fashion.
rows: Single Redis `SET NX PX`
One in-memory primary; expiry by its clock
Simple, fast, fine for efficiency locks; auto-expiry gives liveness
Async replicas can both grant same lock after failover; clock jump breaks TTL; no fencing counter without extra work
Quorum Redis (Redlock-style)
Majority of N independent instances, with validity-time deduction
Survives minority failure without full consensus engine
Still depends on wall-clock bounds and timing assumptions; needs fencing anyway; operational cost of N nodes for weak gain — prefer real consensus if you pay quorum cost
ZooKeeper / etcd (ephemeral sequential nodes)
Consensus log; session expiry deletes node; ordering gives fencing
Strong consistency, session-based liveness, natural monotonic revision for fencing; recipe libraries handle herding
Higher latency and operational weight; session timeout is the same TTL trade-off in new clothes; clients must handle session loss as permanent fence invalidation
Database advisory / row lease
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE owner/token`
No new infra; transactions give atomic acquire; fencing column is natural
Lock table becomes hotspot and failover risk; TTL needs sweeper job which itself needs leadership; throughput caps early
K8s Lease / single-scheduler pinning
One object, one writer via API optimistic concurrency
Good enough for run-once controllers and cron without new systems
API server is the SPOF in practice; lease durations are coarse; not a general mutual-exclusion primitive

blocks.text: Say this with a spine: **if you need correctness, use ZooKeeper/etcd or a transactional store and still add fencing — if you only need efficiency, use single Redis or the database you already run.** Running five Redis nodes to avoid operating etcd is the worst of both worlds: you pay quorum complexity without getting a consensus log or a trustworthy fencing counter. Conversely, dragging etcd into a dedup-email path is resume-driven design. Name the trade-off out loud: consistency and operability cost latency and headcount.
How it fails in production

Distributed locks fail in exactly three shapes: **two holders at once, no holder ever, or a holder that cannot make progress.** Two-at-once comes from expiry during a pause, clock skew, or an unsafe release deleting a successor. Never-available comes from a TTL far longer than mean time to crash, a renewal thread that died silently, or a lock service partitioned away from every worker. No-progress comes from forgetting timeouts on the wait path: fifty workers block forever on a key whose owner is stuck in a downstream call, then thunder back when it releases. All three look identical from the outside at first — latency climbs, then duplicates or gaps appear in downstream data. Your instrumentation must distinguish them: emit `lock.hold_time`, `lock.wait_time`, `lock.renew_fail`, and `fence.rejected` as first-class metrics, or you will misdiagnose a fencing rejection as a database error.

rows: Duplicate side effects: two emails, double charge
Lease expired mid-work; paused holder + successor both active
Hold time vs TTL; GC pause logs; are writes fenced?
Successor's lock vanishes, both proceed
Stale client `DEL` without token compare
Client library release path; switch to Lua compare-delete
Job stalls for full TTL after crash
TTL too long; no heartbeat; renewal thread blocked
Renewal success rate; shorten TTL + add heartbeat; add wait timeout
Split brain after Redis failover
Replica promoted without lock state; two primaries granted
Replication mode; for correctness work, move to consensus store
Workers pile up, then stampede
Unbounded blocking wait, no jitter or deadline
Wait-queue depth; add try-lock with deadline + jittered backoff
Fencing rejections spike
Clock skew or chronic slowness causing superseded writes

blocks.title: The GC-pause interleaving you must draw on a whiteboard
blocks.text: Holder A acquires with 10s TTL. At 8s it pauses for 12s. TTL fires at 10s. B acquires, writes with fence `7`. A wakes at 20s and writes with fence `6`. **Without fencing, A's write silently clobbers B's.** With fencing, storage rejects `6 < 7` and A must re-acquire. If you cannot explain this timeline, do not claim your design is safe.
What to say when they ask about distributed transactions

Locks do not make microservice writes transactional. Holding a lock across two services and two databases gives you **distributed mutual exclusion with none of atomicity, isolation, or rollback** — a slow, deadlock-prone 2PC without the C. The lock serialises entry but each store still commits independently, so a crash between commit one and commit two leaves partial state that no lease expiry will heal. Prefer **idempotent consumers + outbox + saga/compensation** for multi-step workflows, and reserve the lock for the narrow span where true single-writer ordering is required: electing the saga driver, guarding a non-idempotent leg, or serialising access to a legacy system that cannot do conditional writes. Keep the critical section tiny, never call another network service while holding a correctness lock unless the callee also checks the fence token. Every millisecond under lock is availability you borrowed from every other contender.
How it shows up in the interview

items.title: Name the bucket first
items.text: Ask what breaks if two holders exist. Duplicate cron run means efficiency — propose single Redis try-lock with deadline. Money movement means correctness — say so and demand fencing. Interviewers score this split immediately.

items.title: Draw acquire, renew, release with tokens
items.text: Show random owner token, TTL, heartbeat loop, and atomic compare-delete. State the TTL trade-off: short recovers fast but risks false expiry, long is stable but wedges on crash.

items.title: Volunteer the failure timeline
items.text: Walk the GC-pause interleaving unprompted. Then add fencing: lock service issues monotonic tokens, storage rejects stale ones. This is the signal for senior+.

items.title: Compare two implementations and reject one
items.text: Pick single Redis versus etcd/ZooKeeper, justify by consistency need and ops cost. Explicitly reject quorum-without-consensus if correctness matters. Have an opinion.

items.title: Bound the critical section
items.text: Give wait timeout, hold timeout, jittered backoff, and metrics. Say what you never do under lock: fan out to downstream RPCs, hold across sagas, or block forever.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that fail candidates

items: **`SET NX PX` alone is safe if the TTL is long enough.** No — any finite TTL can expire mid-work, and infinite TTL wedges on crash. Length tunes probability, fencing provides safety.
**Releasing with `DEL` is fine.** Only with a token compare. Naked `DEL` lets a stale holder murder its successor.
**Redlock gives consensus-level safety.** It gives availability against minority failure under timing assumptions. Without fencing at the resource, dual ownership is still possible.
**A lock makes scattered writes atomic.** It serialises *entry*, not *commit*. Crash between two stores still leaves partial effects — you need outbox/saga for atomicity.
**Blocking wait is simpler and safe.** Unbounded wait turns one stuck holder into a fleet-wide stall plus stampede. Always use try-lock with deadline, backoff, and jitter.
**Fencing tokens can come from wall-clock timestamps.** Clocks skew. Tokens must be monotonic from the lock service: sequence node, log revision, or atomic increment.

blocks.text: When to use it, when to walk away

blocks.caption: Default to avoiding the lock; earn it with a reason.
headers: Avoid it — do this instead when
rows: Exactly one cron/scheduler must fire despite N replicas
Work is idempotent — allow duplicates and dedup downstream
One writer must drive a legacy file, device, or API without conditional writes
Store supports compare-and-set / conditional write — use optimistic concurrency directly
Electing a driver for a short, well-bounded step
Whole saga needs atomicity — use outbox + saga with compensation, not a giant lock
Suppressing duplicate expensive computation across fleet
Contention is high and sustained — partition/shard the work instead of serialising it
Bridging to a system that cannot fence — as efficiency aid only
Correctness is required but resource cannot check tokens — redesign the resource; no lock can save you

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **Use short leases with owner-checked release for liveness, and enforce safety with monotonic fencing tokens at the resource — locks order access, fencing prevents corruption, and neither replaces transactions.**
